austria.intro: Austria sends a steady trickle of people to Ireland rather than a flood, most of them arriving for jobs in tech, pharma, finance and engineering, or for a year or two of English-language study and university exchange. Many come because an Irish office of an international employer offered a role that suited them, and stay because the work culture feels more relaxed than expected. Others follow an Irish partner home after meeting them abroad. The thing that most surprises Austrians is how informal Irish workplaces are, with first names for everyone and very little ceremony.
austria.community: The Austrian community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, concentrated in Dublin with a scattering in Cork and Galway. Newcomers tend to find each other through the embassy's cultural events, German-speaking Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Stammtisch meetups and the wider German-speaking circles that Austrians, Germans and Swiss share.
austria.contrast: You will miss the mountains and the crisp winters, and the grey mild dampness takes getting used to. Renting is less regulated and more competitive than at home, and you will rarely see a rental contract that lasts as long as an Austrian one. Cards are accepted almost everywhere, shops open late and on Sundays, and pubs replace the Kaffeehaus as the place where social life happens.
austria.language: Most Austrians arrive with strong school English and a good ear, though Irish accents and speed of speech can take a few weeks to tune into. Employers will judge you on the interview rather than a certificate, while universities and professional bodies may still ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs, but nobody expects you to speak it.

belgium.intro: Belgium and Ireland are both small, open, trading countries with a long habit of working in Brussels-style multilingual offices, so Belgians slot easily into Dublin's tech, finance, pharma and EU-facing consultancy jobs. Many come through internal transfers at international firms, others for a master's degree or a stint improving their English, and a fair number for love. The surprise for most Belgians is the pub as the centre of everything: work drinks, birthdays and even job interviews of a sort happen over a pint rather than a long lunch.
belgium.community: Belgians in Ireland form a small but well-organised community, largely in Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People meet through the embassy's national day and cultural events, Flemish and francophone Facebook groups, Belgian beer evenings and the broader French-speaking and Dutch-speaking circles that overlap with neighbours from France and the Netherlands.
belgium.contrast: The climate is similar to Flanders, only windier and a little wetter, so the adjustment is gentler than for most. Rents in Dublin are high and leases short compared with Belgium, and buying groceries and eating out costs noticeably more. Bread and beer will disappoint you at first, tipping is modest and optional, and driving on the left with roundabouts everywhere takes a week of concentration.
belgium.language: Belgians from both language communities usually have good working English, and Irish employers hire on the strength of the interview rather than asking for a test score. If you are registering with a professional body or applying to a university, expect a formal English requirement. Irish is on signs and announcements but is never needed.

bulgaria.intro: Bulgaria has a long-standing pattern of people heading west for work, and Ireland has become one of the preferred destinations because the jobs are in English and the pay is good relative to home. Bulgarians arrive for roles in tech support and software, construction, hospitality, healthcare, logistics and manufacturing, and increasingly for university places. Families often follow once one person is settled. The thing that surprises most Bulgarians is how much of the country is rural and green, and how quickly Dublin gives way to fields and sea.
bulgaria.community: The Bulgarian community in Ireland has grown steadily and is now well established, centred on Dublin but present in Cork, Limerick and smaller towns with factories and hotels. People connect through Bulgarian Orthodox church gatherings, weekend language schools for children, folk dance groups, Facebook and Viber groups and the embassy's national holiday events.
bulgaria.contrast: Winters are milder than Sofia's but darker and wetter, and the lack of proper summer heat is the biggest climate shock. Renting is expensive and finding a place is competitive, so many share houses at first. Groceries and eating out cost more than at home, cards are used for almost everything, and pubs rather than cafés or home gatherings are where you socialise with colleagues.
bulgaria.language: English levels among Bulgarians moving to Ireland vary widely, from fluent tech graduates to people who learn on the job in hospitality or construction. Irish employers will not usually ask for an IELTS score, but nursing, medical and other professional registration bodies and universities do. Irish is on road signs but is not needed.

croatia.intro: Croatia joined the EU relatively recently and Ireland quickly became one of the most popular destinations for Croatians looking for work abroad in English. People come for jobs in construction, hospitality, healthcare, tech support, logistics and pharma manufacturing, and many young graduates come first for a season and then stay. Family reunification follows once one person has a stable job. What surprises Croatians most is how friendly and chatty strangers are, from bus drivers to shop staff, in a way that feels familiar but even more relaxed.
croatia.community: Croatians form a sizeable and fairly recent community, spread across Dublin, Cork, Limerick and towns with big employers rather than concentrated in one area. Newcomers find each other through Catholic Mass in Croatian, football and sports clubs, Croatian cultural associations, Facebook and WhatsApp groups and the embassy's events around national holidays.
croatia.contrast: The biggest adjustment is the weather: no Adriatic summer, long dark winters, and rain that comes and goes all day. Rents are high and housing is tight, so many people start in shared accommodation. Groceries and coffee cost more, cash has almost disappeared in favour of cards, and evenings are spent in pubs rather than on café terraces or the riva.
croatia.language: Most younger Croatians arrive with good English from school, television and tourism work, and Irish employers hire on the interview rather than a certificate. Healthcare and other regulated professions and universities will ask for a formal English test. Irish appears on signs and public notices but is not required.

cyprus.intro: Cyprus and Ireland share the same island-nation feel, a Commonwealth-era link to British education and a habit of sending young people abroad to study. Cypriots move to Ireland for university degrees, especially medicine, law and business, for jobs in finance, tech, pharma and shipping-related services, and for the chance to work in English in the EU. Many first come as students and stay on after graduating. The thing that most surprises Cypriots is how early the day ends in winter, with darkness by mid-afternoon.
cyprus.community: The Cypriot community in Ireland is small, mostly students and professionals in Dublin, with a strong overlap with the wider Greek community. People meet through the Greek Orthodox parish, university Hellenic and Cypriot societies, Facebook groups and events organised by the embassy and the Greek and Cypriot associations.
cyprus.contrast: Coming from a country where sun is guaranteed, the Irish climate is the hardest part, and most Cypriots find the wind harder than the rain. Rents are high and flats often unfurnished or oddly furnished compared with home. Eating out is expensive, tipping is light, pubs replace late-night tavernas and cafés, and shops close far earlier than you are used to.
cyprus.language: Cypriots typically arrive with strong English from school and the British-style education system, so working and socialising is easy from day one. Employers will not ask for a test, but universities and professional bodies may still require one. Irish is on signs but you will never need to use it.

the-czech-republic.intro: The Czech Republic sends people to Ireland mainly for work in tech, customer support in multiple languages, pharma and medtech manufacturing, engineering and hospitality, along with a steady stream of students improving their English. Many Czechs first arrive through a job at an international company's Dublin or Cork office, and a good number come for a year and stay much longer. What surprises most Czechs is the price and quality of beer in Irish pubs, which are nothing like a Prague hospoda, and the fact that people talk to strangers everywhere.
the-czech-republic.community: The Czech community in Ireland is medium-sized and well established, mostly in Dublin with groups in Cork and Galway. Newcomers find each other through Czech and Slovak Facebook groups, the Czech school for children, embassy cultural events, film evenings and shared gatherings with the closely linked Slovak community.
the-czech-republic.contrast: Irish winters are milder but far darker and wetter than Czech ones, and summers rarely get properly hot. Renting is more expensive and less secure than at home, and grocery shopping costs more. Cards are used for everything, Sunday trading is normal, tipping is optional, and the pub is the default social venue for colleagues and friends alike.
the-czech-republic.language: Younger Czechs usually arrive with solid English, and Irish employers hire on the interview and CV rather than a test score, although universities and professional registration bodies do ask for one. Irish is on signs and public transport announcements but nobody expects you to speak it.

denmark.intro: Denmark and Ireland are both small, outward-looking countries with strong pharma and tech sectors, and Danes tend to move to Ireland through international employers, for research posts at Irish universities, or for a change of scene in an English-speaking capital. Some come for a partner, others for the music and outdoor life on the west coast. The surprise for most Danes is how loose Irish timekeeping and planning can be, with meetings, dinners and even buses treated as suggestions rather than fixed points.
denmark.community: The Danish community in Ireland is small, mostly professionals in Dublin with some in Cork, and it overlaps heavily with the wider Scandinavian circle. People meet through the embassy's cultural events, Nordic Facebook and WhatsApp groups, church and Christmas gatherings and the informal Scandinavian meetups that Danes, Swedes and Norwegians share.
denmark.contrast: The climate is similar to Denmark's, wetter and windier but with milder winters, so the change is mild. Renting is the shock: Dublin housing is expensive, leases are short and standards vary widely compared with Danish rentals. Cycling infrastructure is thinner, cars drive on the left, and social life happens in pubs rather than at home over a long dinner.
denmark.language: Danes almost always arrive with fluent English and slip into Irish workplaces without difficulty, though the accent and indirect way of saying no can take time to read. Employers will not ask for a certificate, but universities and professional bodies may. Irish appears on signs but is never required.

estonia.intro: Estonia has a strong digital culture, and Estonians moving to Ireland are often software developers, product and data specialists or people working in customer support and finance at the big Dublin tech firms. Others come for university, for hospitality and construction work, or for a partner. Ireland's English-speaking workplaces and EU freedom of movement make it a natural step. What surprises most Estonians is how much paper and in-person administration still exists in Ireland, in a country that otherwise feels modern.
estonia.community: The Estonian community in Ireland is small but active, based mostly in Dublin with a few people in Cork and Galway. Newcomers connect through Estonian Facebook and WhatsApp groups, the Estonian school and Independence Day gatherings, embassy events and shared Baltic and Nordic meetups with Latvians, Lithuanians and Finns.
estonia.contrast: Irish winters are less cold but darker in feel because of the constant cloud, and there is no proper snow or summer light. Renting is expensive and competitive, and Estonians used to quick online everything will find Irish landlords and services slower. Cards are accepted everywhere, and socialising means the pub rather than the sauna or a quiet gathering at home.
estonia.language: Estonians generally arrive with strong English, especially in tech, and Irish employers will judge you on the interview rather than a test. Universities and professional registration bodies are the ones that ask for a formal score. Irish is on signs and announcements but is not needed.

finland.intro: Finland sends a small but steady number of people to Ireland, most of them working in tech, gaming, telecoms and pharma, doing research at Irish universities or arriving with an Irish partner. Others come for the music, the coastline and a friendlier climate than they expected from an island in the north Atlantic. Ireland's relaxed, sociable working culture is often the draw. The thing that most surprises Finns is small talk: shop staff, taxi drivers and colleagues chat constantly, and silence in company is treated as something to fix.
finland.community: The Finnish community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, centred on Dublin with a few families in Cork and Galway. People find each other through the Finnish church's seasonal events, the embassy's Independence Day reception, Nordic Facebook and WhatsApp groups and sauna evenings organised through the wider Scandinavian circle.
finland.contrast: Winters are much milder and greener than at home but just as dark, and the lack of snow and proper cold can feel strange. Irish housing is expensive and often poorly insulated compared with Finnish standards, and rental leases are shorter. Cards are used everywhere, pubs replace the sauna as the place to unwind, and Sunday opening is normal.
finland.language: Finns typically arrive with excellent English and adapt quickly, although the Irish habit of indirect answers and constant chat can take a while to decode. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs but nobody expects you to speak it.

france.intro: France has one of the largest European communities in Ireland, drawn by jobs in tech, finance, pharma, aviation and hospitality, by Irish universities and by the long tradition of young French people spending a year in Dublin to perfect their English. Many arrive on internal transfers or as new graduates and find the career ladder faster and flatter than at home. Couples and families follow. The surprise for most French people is the Irish approach to food and meals: lunch at the desk, dinner early, and the pub rather than the table as the centre of social life.
france.community: The French community in Ireland is large and long-established, with a strong presence in Dublin and smaller groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick. Newcomers find each other through the Alliance Française, the French school and lycée network, French Catholic Mass, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, sports clubs and regular consulate and cultural events.
france.contrast: The climate is greyer and wetter than most of France and the winter days are short, but summers are long and light. Renting is more expensive and less protected than in France, and groceries and eating out cost more, with fewer bakeries and markets. Tipping is light, shops open on Sundays, and the working day starts and ends earlier with a much shorter lunch.
france.language: French speakers arrive with a wide range of English, and many use their first year in Ireland precisely to become fluent. Irish employers rarely ask for a test score, but universities and professional bodies do. Irish appears on signs and announcements alongside English but is not needed in daily life.

germany.intro: Germany has one of the biggest and oldest continental communities in Ireland, built on jobs in tech, pharma, medtech, finance, aviation leasing and engineering, on strong university links and on the many Germans who came for a year of English and never left. Internal transfers within international firms are common, and Germans are well represented in Dublin's multinational offices and Cork's pharma plants. The thing that most surprises Germans is how flexible Irish rules and timings are, and how much gets done through a chat rather than a form.
germany.community: The German community in Ireland is large, long-established and spread across Dublin, Cork, Galway and Limerick, with a German school, Lutheran church and Goethe-Institut providing focal points in the capital. People meet through Stammtisch groups, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, sports clubs, embassy events and the wider German-speaking circle shared with Austrians and Swiss.
germany.contrast: The Irish climate is milder but wetter and darker than Germany's, with far fewer proper summer days. Renting is the big adjustment: leases are short, tenant protections weaker, flats often come furnished and prices in Dublin are high. Bread and recycling systems will disappoint you, cards are used everywhere, shops open on Sundays and the pub replaces the Verein as the place where community happens.
germany.language: Germans usually arrive with strong English, and Irish employers hire on the interview and CV rather than asking for a test. Universities and professional registration bodies may still require a formal English score. Irish is on signs and public transport but is not needed at all.

greece.intro: Greece sends many young professionals to Ireland, especially in tech, finance, pharma, engineering and academia, alongside doctors and nurses, hospitality workers and students at Irish universities. Ireland's English-language job market and EU access make it a natural choice for Greeks looking to build a career abroad, and many arrive after finishing a master's degree. Families and partners follow once someone is settled. What surprises Greeks most is how early evenings end: dinner at six or seven and pubs closing while a Greek night out would just be starting.
greece.community: The Greek community in Ireland is medium-sized and growing, concentrated in Dublin with active groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick. Newcomers find each other through the Greek Orthodox parish, Greek community associations, university Hellenic societies, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Greek music nights and embassy events around national holidays.
greece.contrast: The lack of sun and the long dark winters are the hardest part, and many Greeks say the wind bothers them more than the rain. Renting is expensive and competitive, and eating out and groceries cost more than at home with far less fresh produce variety. Tipping is optional, cards are used for everything, and pubs and early dinners replace tavernas and long late meals.
greece.language: Most Greeks moving to Ireland have good English from school and private lessons, and Irish employers hire on the interview rather than a certificate. Medical, nursing and other registration bodies and universities will ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs and announcements but is not needed.

hungary.intro: Hungary sends a steady flow of people to Ireland for work in tech and multilingual customer support, pharma and medtech manufacturing, healthcare, construction, hospitality and logistics, along with students and young graduates keen to work in English. Many come through the Dublin offices of international companies, and a good number move as families once one person has settled. The thing that most surprises Hungarians is the informality of Irish life: first names everywhere, casual dress at work and strangers who chat as if they know you.
hungary.community: The Hungarian community in Ireland is medium-sized and well established, mainly in Dublin with groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick. People connect through Hungarian Catholic and Reformed church gatherings, weekend Hungarian schools for children, folk dance and cultural groups, Facebook groups and events organised by the embassy and Hungarian associations.
hungary.contrast: Irish winters are milder than Hungarian ones but darker and wetter, and summers rarely bring real heat. Renting is expensive and finding a place takes effort, so sharing is common at first. Groceries and eating out cost more, thermal baths and long café afternoons are replaced by pubs, cards are used for everything and shops open on Sundays.
hungary.language: English levels among Hungarians vary from fluent tech and finance graduates to people who improve on the job in hospitality or construction. Irish employers hire on the interview and CV, while universities and professional registration bodies ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs but nobody expects you to speak it.

iceland.intro: Iceland and Ireland are both small Atlantic islands with a shared Norse and Celtic history, and Icelanders move to Ireland for jobs in tech, finance, aviation and pharma, for university study and research, or simply for a bigger city and a warmer, greener version of home. Many arrive through international employers or an Irish partner. The country is small enough to feel familiar and big enough to offer more choice. The thing that most surprises Icelanders is how far Ireland's cities sprawl and how much time people spend commuting.
iceland.community: The Icelandic community in Ireland is very small, mostly professionals and students in Dublin. People tend to find each other through Nordic Facebook and WhatsApp groups, gatherings organised through the honorary consulate and the wider Scandinavian circle, and Icelandic national day and Christmas events shared with Danes, Norwegians and Finns.
iceland.contrast: The climate feels like a gentler Iceland: milder, greener and with more rain than wind, and with proper trees. Renting is expensive and competitive, and Icelanders used to geothermal heating will notice cold, damp houses. Cards are used everywhere, alcohol is sold in ordinary shops and pubs, and the working day is a little less intense than at home.
iceland.language: Icelanders almost always arrive with fluent English and settle into Irish workplaces without difficulty. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs and announcements but is never needed.

italy.intro: Italy is one of the largest sources of new arrivals in Ireland, with Italians working across tech, finance, pharma, medtech, hospitality, universities and healthcare, and many arriving first for a year of English or a master's degree. Young graduates often find that Irish employers hire faster and promote earlier than at home, and Dublin's multinationals recruit Italian speakers steadily. Families and partners follow. What surprises Italians most is Irish meal culture: lunch eaten at the desk in minutes, dinner early, and coffee that rarely meets Italian standards.
italy.community: The Italian community in Ireland is large and long-established, concentrated in Dublin with active groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick. Newcomers find each other through the Italian Cultural Institute, Italian Catholic Mass, football and sports clubs, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, aperitivo meetups and consulate and community events.
italy.contrast: The climate is the hardest adjustment, with long dark winters and mild summers that rarely feel like summer. Renting is more expensive and less protected than in Italy, and groceries and eating out cost considerably more. Cards are used everywhere, tipping is light, shops open on Sundays, and the pub takes the place of the piazza and the long evening passeggiata.
italy.language: Italians arrive with a wide spread of English, and many spend their first year in Ireland becoming fluent. Irish employers hire on the interview and CV rather than a test, but universities and professional registration bodies do require a formal score. Irish is on signs but is not needed in daily life.

latvia.intro: Latvia has a long tradition of people moving to Ireland for work, first in construction, manufacturing, logistics, hospitality and farming, and increasingly in tech, finance and customer support at Dublin's international companies. Many arrive with a job already arranged through friends or family who came earlier, and children often join once parents are settled. Irish universities also draw Latvian students. The thing that most surprises Latvians is how open and talkative Irish people are, and how much of daily life is arranged through a friendly word rather than a rule.
latvia.community: The Latvian community in Ireland is large and long-established, spread across Dublin, Cork, Limerick and many smaller towns with factories and farms. People find each other through Latvian schools and cultural associations, Lutheran and Catholic congregations, folk dance and choir groups, Facebook and WhatsApp groups and embassy events around independence day.
latvia.contrast: Irish winters are much milder than Latvian ones but darker in feel because of the cloud, and there is no snow or real summer heat. Renting is expensive and competitive, so many people share at first. Groceries and eating out cost more, cards are used for almost everything, and pubs rather than home gatherings are where colleagues socialise.
latvia.language: English levels among Latvians range from fluent graduates in tech to people who learn quickly on the job, and many also speak Russian, which some employers value. Irish employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs but is not needed.

lithuania.intro: Lithuania sends a large number of people to Ireland, originally for construction, manufacturing, logistics, hospitality and food processing, and now increasingly for tech, finance, healthcare and customer support in Dublin's multinationals. Many Lithuanians arrive to join relatives or friends who came years earlier and helped them find work and housing. Children grow up bilingual and families often settle for good. What surprises most Lithuanians is the Irish habit of making conversation with anyone, anywhere, and how much gets done through personal contacts.
lithuania.community: The Lithuanian community in Ireland is one of the largest and most established, present in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and dozens of smaller towns. Newcomers connect through Lithuanian Catholic parishes, weekend Lithuanian schools, basketball and football clubs, cultural associations, Facebook and WhatsApp groups and embassy events on national holidays.
lithuania.contrast: Winters are milder but wetter and darker than Lithuanian ones, and summers rarely get hot. Renting is expensive and finding a place is competitive, so many start in shared houses. Groceries and eating out cost more, cards are used everywhere, shops open on Sundays and the pub replaces the sauna and the countryside gathering as the default way to socialise.
lithuania.language: English levels among Lithuanians vary widely, from fluent professionals to people who improve on the job, and many also speak Russian or Polish. Irish employers hire on the interview rather than a test, while universities and professional registration bodies ask for a formal score. Irish appears on signs but is not required.

luxembourg.intro: Luxembourg is a small country whose people are used to working in several languages across borders, so Luxembourgers fit naturally into Dublin's finance, funds, tech and EU-facing consultancy jobs. Some move on internal transfers within international firms, others for Irish universities or for a partner, and a few because they want a bigger, English-speaking city with a similar open economy. The thing that most surprises Luxembourgers is how informal and chatty Irish workplaces are, and how quickly colleagues become friends over a pint.
luxembourg.community: Luxembourgers in Ireland are a very small community, mostly professionals in Dublin, and they usually join the larger francophone, German-speaking and Belgian circles rather than forming their own. People meet through embassy and honorary consulate events, EU-related networks, Facebook groups and the shared gatherings of neighbouring countries.
luxembourg.contrast: The climate is similar but windier and wetter than at home, with fewer cold snaps and less snow. Renting is expensive and less regulated, and groceries and eating out cost more than in Luxembourg, though wages in similar sectors are comparable. Cards are used everywhere, public transport is not free, shops open on Sundays and social life revolves around the pub.
luxembourg.language: Luxembourgers usually arrive with fluent English on top of Luxembourgish, French and German, and settle into Irish workplaces easily. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs but is never needed.

malta.intro: Malta and Ireland share a lot: small islands, Catholic heritage, a British past, English as a working language and economies built on services. Maltese people move to Ireland for jobs in tech, gaming, finance, pharma, healthcare and hospitality, for Irish universities and for the chance of a bigger job market without changing language. Many come as young graduates or nurses and doctors. What surprises most Maltese is how green and spacious Ireland feels, with countryside and long drives instead of a whole country you can cross in an hour.
malta.community: The Maltese community in Ireland is small but friendly, mostly in Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People find each other through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Catholic parishes, events organised by the embassy and Maltese associations, and the broader Mediterranean circle shared with Italians and Cypriots.
malta.contrast: The weather is the hardest part: long dark winters, constant rain and a summer that would feel like a Maltese spring. Renting is expensive and competitive, though housing is generally larger. Eating out and groceries cost more, tipping is light, shops open on Sundays and pubs replace the village festa and café as the place to gather.
malta.language: Maltese people are usually fully bilingual in Maltese and English, so working and socialising in Ireland is immediate, though Irish slang and accents differ from the British English you learned. Employers will not ask for a test, and even professional bodies often accept Maltese education. Irish appears on signs but is never needed.

the-netherlands.intro: The Netherlands and Ireland are close neighbours by air and trade, and Dutch people move to Ireland for jobs in tech, finance, aviation leasing, pharma, agriculture and consultancy, for Irish universities and research, or for a partner. Many arrive through international employers who want Dutch speakers in Dublin, and others come for the slower pace and the coastline of the west. The thing that most surprises the Dutch is how indirect Irish communication is, with no blunt no and plenty of reading between the lines.
the-netherlands.community: The Dutch community in Ireland is medium-sized and well established, mostly in Dublin with groups in Cork, Galway and rural areas where Dutch farmers settled. Newcomers find each other through Dutch Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Koningsdag and Sinterklaas events, the Dutch church and school activities, embassy events and hockey and football clubs.
the-netherlands.contrast: The climate is similar but wetter, windier and hillier, and cycling is far less easy and safe than at home. Renting is expensive and leases are short, and the cost of groceries and eating out is higher. Cards are used everywhere, cars drive on the left, shops open on Sundays, and the pub is the social venue rather than a borrel at home or the office.
the-netherlands.language: Dutch people arrive with near-fluent English and slot into Irish workplaces without difficulty, though Irish directness runs the other way from Dutch directness and can take time to read. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a test. Irish is on signs but is never needed.

norway.intro: Norway sends a small but steady number of people to Ireland for work in tech, energy, finance, pharma and shipping-related services, for research posts and degrees at Irish universities, and quite often for a partner met abroad. Some come for the music and the west coast landscapes that feel like a greener version of home. Ireland's English-speaking workplaces make it an easy transfer within international firms. What surprises Norwegians most is how relaxed and sociable Irish work culture is, with long lunches and after-work pints that would be rare at home.
norway.community: The Norwegian community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, centred on Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People connect through the embassy's Constitution Day celebrations, the Norwegian church's seasonal events, Nordic Facebook and WhatsApp groups and the shared Scandinavian meetups with Danes, Swedes and Finns.
norway.contrast: Winters are much milder and greener than Norway's but still dark and grey, with far less snow and no real summer light. Renting is expensive and leases are short, and housing insulation can feel poor compared with Norwegian standards. Cards are used everywhere, alcohol is cheap by Norwegian standards and freely sold, and the pub is the centre of social life.
norway.language: Norwegians almost always arrive with fluent English and adapt quickly, although Irish accents and indirect answers can take a while to tune into. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs and announcements but is never needed.

poland.intro: Poland is the largest source of new residents in Ireland from continental Europe, and the movement has been going on long enough that many Polish families have children born and raised in Ireland. People come for work in construction, manufacturing, logistics, hospitality, healthcare, retail and increasingly tech, finance and customer support in Dublin's multinationals. Many arrive to join relatives or friends who came earlier. What surprises most Poles is how relaxed Irish people are about time and planning, and how much daily life runs on friendly chat rather than formality.
poland.community: The Polish community in Ireland is very large and deeply established, present in every city and most towns, with Polish shops, Catholic Mass in Polish, weekend schools and cultural centres. Newcomers find each other easily through parishes, Polish schools, football clubs, Facebook and WhatsApp groups and community events organised by Polish associations and the embassy.
poland.contrast: Irish winters are milder than Polish ones but darker and wetter, and summers rarely bring real heat. Renting is expensive and competitive, so many people start in shared houses. Groceries and eating out cost more, though Polish shops are everywhere for familiar products. Cards are used for everything, shops open on Sundays and the pub replaces the home gathering as the default social venue.
poland.language: English among Poles moving to Ireland ranges from fluent graduates to people who learn on the job, and the size of the community means you can get by in Polish at first. Irish employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional registration bodies ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs but not needed.

portugal.intro: Portugal sends a growing number of people to Ireland, particularly nurses and doctors, tech workers and customer support staff at Dublin's international companies, engineers in pharma and construction, and hospitality workers. Young graduates come for better pay and faster career progression, and many first arrive for an English course or a master's degree. Families and partners follow once someone has settled. The thing that most surprises the Portuguese is how early everything happens: lunch at noon, dinner at six, and the pubs busy while a Lisbon evening would just be getting started.
portugal.community: The Portuguese community in Ireland is medium-sized and growing, mostly in Dublin with groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick, and it overlaps with the large Brazilian community. People meet through Portuguese Catholic Mass, football clubs, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Portuguese cultural associations and events organised by the embassy and the Instituto Camões.
portugal.contrast: The lack of sun and the long dark winters are the hardest adjustment, and summers feel like a mild Portuguese spring. Renting is expensive and competitive, and groceries, coffee and eating out cost much more than at home. Cards are used everywhere, tipping is light, shops open on Sundays, and pubs and early nights replace cafés and long late dinners.
portugal.language: Most younger Portuguese arrive with good English from school and television, and Irish employers hire on the interview rather than a certificate. Nursing, medical and other registration bodies and universities do ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

romania.intro: Romania is one of the largest sources of new arrivals in Ireland, with Romanians working in construction, healthcare, tech, hospitality, logistics, manufacturing and retail, and a growing number in finance and multilingual customer support in Dublin. Many come to join family or friends who arrived earlier and helped find a first job and room. Irish universities also draw Romanian students, and children often grow up fully bilingual. What surprises most Romanians is how quickly Irish people warm to strangers and how easily colleagues become friends.
romania.community: The Romanian community in Ireland is large and well established, present in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and many smaller towns. Newcomers find each other through Romanian Orthodox parishes, Romanian shops and weekend schools, cultural associations, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, football clubs and events organised by the embassy and consulate.
romania.contrast: Irish winters are milder than Romanian ones but darker and wetter, and summers rarely bring real heat. Renting is expensive and competitive, so shared houses are common at first. Groceries and eating out cost more, though Romanian and Eastern European shops are widespread. Cards are used for almost everything, shops open on Sundays and pubs replace home and terrace gatherings as the way to socialise.
romania.language: English among Romanians moving to Ireland ranges from fluent graduates in tech and healthcare to people who improve on the job. Irish employers hire on the interview, while nursing, medical and other registration bodies and universities ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs but nobody expects you to speak it.

slovakia.intro: Slovakia sends a steady flow of people to Ireland, mainly for jobs in tech and multilingual customer support, pharma and medtech manufacturing, healthcare, construction, logistics and hospitality, along with students and young graduates who want to work in English. Many arrive through Dublin's international companies or to join friends and family who came earlier. Some come for a season and stay for years. What surprises most Slovaks is the Irish way of talking to everyone, from bus drivers to shop staff, and how much daily life depends on being friendly rather than formal.
slovakia.community: The Slovak community in Ireland is medium-sized and well established, concentrated in Dublin with groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick, and closely linked with the Czech community. People find each other through Slovak Catholic Mass, weekend Slovak schools, football and hockey clubs, Facebook and WhatsApp groups and embassy cultural events.
slovakia.contrast: Irish winters are milder but darker and wetter than Slovak ones, with no real snow or summer heat. Renting is expensive and competitive, so sharing is common at first. Groceries and eating out cost more, cards are used for everything, shops open on Sundays and the pub takes the place of the cottage weekend and the home gathering as the default social venue.
slovakia.language: Younger Slovaks usually arrive with solid English, and Irish employers hire on the interview and CV rather than a test score. Universities and professional registration bodies do ask for a formal English requirement. Irish appears on signs but is not required.

slovenia.intro: Slovenia is a small country with a strong education system, and Slovenians moving to Ireland are often engineers, software developers, pharma and medtech specialists, researchers at Irish universities or young graduates keen to work in English. Others come for hospitality jobs, for a partner or for a year abroad that turns into longer. Ireland's international companies and EU freedom of movement make the move straightforward. What surprises most Slovenians is how far you are from mountains and how much time you spend in the car, given how used you are to short distances at home.
slovenia.community: The Slovenian community in Ireland is small but active, mostly professionals in Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People connect through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, embassy events around national holidays, shared gatherings with Croatians and other neighbouring communities, and informal meetups for hiking and cycling that help ease the missing Alps.
slovenia.contrast: The Irish climate is milder but far greyer and wetter than Slovenia's, with no proper winter snow or summer heat. Renting is expensive and competitive, and groceries and eating out cost more. Cards are used everywhere, shops open on Sundays, tipping is light, and the pub replaces the mountain hut and the coffee terrace as the place to meet friends.
slovenia.language: Slovenians generally arrive with strong English from school and university, and Irish employers hire on the interview rather than a certificate. Universities and professional registration bodies ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs and public transport but is never needed.

spain.intro: Spain is one of the biggest sources of new arrivals in Ireland, with Spaniards working in tech, finance, pharma, healthcare, hospitality and universities, and many arriving first to study English or take a master's degree. Young graduates find Irish employers hire quickly and promote early, and Dublin's multinationals recruit Spanish speakers constantly. Nurses, doctors and engineers follow in large numbers, and partners and families come once someone is settled. What surprises the Spanish most is how early the Irish day ends, with dinner at six and pubs closing while Madrid would still be on its first drink.
spain.community: The Spanish community in Ireland is large and well established, concentrated in Dublin with active groups in Cork, Galway and Limerick. Newcomers find each other through the Instituto Cervantes, Spanish Catholic Mass, football and padel clubs, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, intercambio language meetups and consulate and community events.
spain.contrast: The climate is the hardest part: long dark winters, constant rain and a summer that feels like a mild Spanish spring. Renting is expensive and competitive, and groceries and eating out cost much more with far less fresh produce. Cards are used everywhere, tipping is light, shops open on Sundays and pubs and early nights replace terraces, tapas and long late dinners.
spain.language: Spanish speakers arrive with a wide spread of English, and many spend their first year in Ireland becoming fluent. Irish employers hire on the interview and CV rather than a test, but nursing, medical and other registration bodies and universities require a formal score. Irish is on signs but not needed.

sweden.intro: Sweden sends a small but steady stream of people to Ireland for work in tech, gaming, pharma, finance and telecoms, for research and degrees at Irish universities, and quite often for a partner. Some come for the music, the coastline and a friendlier, less structured working culture than at home. Ireland's English-speaking workplaces make the transfer simple within international firms. The thing that most surprises Swedes is how spontaneous and unplanned Irish social life is, with plans made on the day and evenings that run far later than intended.
sweden.community: The Swedish community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, centred on Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People meet through the Swedish church's Lucia and Midsummer events, the embassy's national day reception, Nordic Facebook and WhatsApp groups and the shared Scandinavian meetups with Danes, Norwegians and Finns.
sweden.contrast: Winters are much milder and greener than Sweden's but still dark and grey, with far less snow and no long summer light. Renting is expensive and leases are short, and Irish houses can feel cold and damp compared with Swedish homes. Cards are used everywhere, alcohol is sold freely in shops and pubs, and social life happens in pubs rather than at home over fika.
sweden.language: Swedes almost always arrive with fluent English and adapt quickly, though the Irish habit of chat and indirect answers can take a while to read. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs but is never needed.

switzerland.intro: Switzerland and Ireland are both small, wealthy countries with strong pharma, finance and tech sectors, and Swiss people move to Ireland mainly through international employers, for Irish universities and research, or for a partner. Some come for a less structured working culture and a more relaxed pace, others for the west coast and the music. Ireland offers English-speaking workplaces and EU access that the Swiss cannot get at home. What surprises most Swiss is how loose Irish timekeeping is, with buses, meetings and dinners all running on a more forgiving clock.
switzerland.community: The Swiss community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, based in Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People connect through the embassy's national day and cultural events, German-speaking and francophone Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Stammtisch meetups and the wider German, Austrian, French and Italian circles that Swiss people slot into.
switzerland.contrast: You will miss the mountains and the crisp winters, and the grey mild dampness can wear on you. Renting is expensive and less regulated than at home, though groceries and eating out are cheaper than in Switzerland. Cards are used everywhere, shops open on Sundays and late evenings, tipping is light, and the pub replaces the mountain hut and the long Sunday walk as the place to meet people.
switzerland.language: Swiss people generally arrive with strong English, whichever language they grew up with, and Irish employers hire on the interview rather than asking for a test. Universities and professional registration bodies may still require a formal English score. Irish appears on signs but is never needed.

albania.intro: Albania sends a steady trickle of people to Ireland rather than a flood, and most come for work in construction, hospitality, care and, increasingly, tech and pharma. Younger Albanians often arrive for English-language study or a postgraduate course and then stay on for a job. Others follow family already settled in Dublin. What surprises many new arrivals is how soft and changeable the weather is: there is rarely a hard winter, but there is rarely a proper summer either, and rain can arrive on any day of the year.
albania.community: The Albanian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated mostly in Dublin with smaller pockets around Cork and Limerick. Newcomers tend to find each other through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, a few cultural associations, and word of mouth among families who have been here a while.
albania.contrast: You will notice the early nights first: shops and cafés close far earlier than in Tirana, and evening life happens in the pub rather than on the street. Card payments are accepted almost everywhere, tipping is modest and optional, and eating out costs noticeably more than at home. Driving is on the left, which takes a few weeks to feel natural.
albania.language: English is widely taught in Albania and many arrivals speak it well, though Irish accents take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a formal test, but universities and professional registration bodies usually do. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

armenia.intro: Armenia has a strong engineering and software tradition, and that is what brings most Armenians to Ireland: roles in tech, data and product at the multinationals around Dublin, alongside a smaller number in finance, universities and healthcare. Some arrive as students and stay, others transfer within a company, and family links tend to follow once one person is established. The thing that surprises many Armenians is the absence of proper seasons: winters are mild and grey rather than snowy, and summers rarely get hot, so the wardrobe you packed is probably wrong.
armenia.community: The Armenian community in Ireland is small and mostly recent, centred on Dublin and largely made up of professionals and students. There is a modest round of cultural and church gatherings, but most newcomers connect through WhatsApp groups, embassy-linked events and the wider Eastern European and Caucasus circles in the city.
armenia.contrast: Rent absorbs a far larger share of income than in Yerevan, and viewings for flats are competitive, so start looking early. Daily life runs on cards rather than cash, restaurants close their kitchens surprisingly early, and the pub takes the social role that the café holds at home. Driving on the left is a real adjustment for the first month.
armenia.language: Armenians in tech and academia usually have solid working English, though fast Irish speech takes a while. Employers judge English at interview rather than by certificate; universities and professional bodies do ask for formal proof. Irish is on signs but not needed.

azerbaijan.intro: Azerbaijan sends a small but growing number of people to Ireland, mostly for postgraduate study, English-language courses and jobs in tech, engineering and finance in Dublin. Many first come as students at Irish universities and stay on once they find work, and a few move for family reasons. The surprise for most Azerbaijanis is the weather: coming from Baku's long hot summers, the constant wind, drizzle and mild grey winters of the Irish coast take real getting used to.
azerbaijan.community: The Azerbaijani community in Ireland is small and relatively new, concentrated in Dublin and made up largely of students and young professionals. People usually find each other through university societies, embassy events, Turkish and wider Caucasus social circles, and Facebook or WhatsApp groups rather than through any large formal organisation.
azerbaijan.contrast: Everything runs on card in Ireland and you will rarely need cash, while tipping is light and mostly reserved for sit-down meals. Groceries cost more than in Baku and eating out considerably more, so most people cook at home during the week. Shops close early, the evening happens in the pub, and driving is on the left.
azerbaijan.language: Azerbaijanis who come for study or tech work usually arrive with good English, but Irish accents can be a shock at first. Employers rarely demand a test score, though universities and professional registration bodies do. Irish is on signs but daily life is in English.

belarus.intro: Belarus has a deep pool of software engineers, and Ireland's tech sector is the main reason Belarusians move here, whether through company transfers, direct hires at the Dublin multinationals or remote roles that turned into relocations. Others come for academic posts, finance jobs or to join family already settled, and a smaller group arrives via English-language study. What most surprises Belarusians is how informal Irish workplaces are: first names all round, flat hierarchies and managers who chat about the weekend before getting to the point.
belarus.community: The Belarusian community in Ireland is small and mostly recent, concentrated in Dublin and made up largely of IT professionals and their families. Newcomers tend to find each other through Telegram and Facebook groups, Russian-speaking social circles, and occasional cultural events, rather than through any long-established association.
belarus.contrast: Winters are far milder than Minsk but darker and wetter, and the lack of snow feels strange rather than pleasant at first. Renting is expensive and competitive, groceries cost more, and almost every purchase is by card. Pubs are the centre of social life, shops shut early, and you drive on the left.
belarus.language: Belarusian tech workers usually arrive with strong written English and improve their spoken fluency quickly, though Irish accents take time. Employers assess English in interview; universities and professional registration bodies are the ones who ask for formal scores. Irish is on signs but not needed.

bosnia-and-herzegovina.intro: Bosnia and Herzegovina has a long habit of sending people abroad for work, and Ireland has become one of the destinations for engineers, healthcare workers, tradespeople and hospitality staff, alongside a growing number in tech and pharma. Some come for postgraduate study or English, others follow relatives already here, and the reason is usually ordinary: better pay, more opportunity, a change of scene. What surprises many Bosnians is the cost of a simple coffee and a night out compared with Sarajevo or Mostar, and how early everything closes.
bosnia-and-herzegovina.community: The Bosnian community in Ireland is small but has been here a while, with families who arrived a generation ago alongside more recent workers, and it is centred on Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through the wider ex-Yugoslav circles, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, mosque and church communities, and football.
bosnia-and-herzegovina.contrast: Coffee culture at home is long and social; in Ireland it is often a takeaway cup on the way somewhere, and the long evening sits happen in the pub instead. Rent is a much bigger share of income, groceries and restaurants cost more, and payments are mostly by card. Winters are milder but darker, and you drive on the left.
bosnia-and-herzegovina.language: Younger Bosnians often arrive with good English from school and television, while others build it on the job. Employers rarely ask for a test certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies will. Irish is on road signs and documents but you do not need it.

georgia.intro: Georgia has become a source of nurses, care workers, hospitality staff and, increasingly, software developers and students heading to Ireland. Many Georgians arrive for English-language study or a master's degree and stay for work, while others come through healthcare recruitment or to join a partner. The reasons are the usual ones: pay, opportunity and a sense of adventure. What tends to surprise Georgians most is the Irish approach to hospitality, warm but low-key, with no expectation of the long feasts and toasts that define a gathering at home.
georgia.community: The Georgian community in Ireland is small and recent, mostly in Dublin with some people in Cork and Galway through healthcare and hospitality jobs. Newcomers find each other through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Orthodox church gatherings, and the wider Eastern European social scene rather than through any large formal organisation.
georgia.contrast: Rent takes a far larger share of a salary than in Tbilisi, and finding a flat is a competition rather than a formality. Eating out is expensive, so socialising happens over pints rather than supra-style dinners, and almost everything is paid by card. Winters are mild but grey, and driving is on the left.
georgia.language: English levels vary widely among Georgians, from fluent graduates to people learning on the job, and Irish accents add a hurdle at first. Employers judge your English in conversation, while universities and professional registration bodies ask for formal results. Irish is on signs, not needed.

kosovo.intro: Kosovo has a young population and a strong tradition of working abroad, and Ireland draws Kosovars into construction, hospitality, care work and, increasingly, tech, where the country's growing IT sector produces plenty of developers. Some arrive for English-language study or university and stay for work; others follow family already here. Better wages and the chance to build something are the usual reasons. What surprises many Kosovars is how quiet Irish evenings are: shops and cafés close early, and the social life that fills the streets of Pristina is tucked away inside pubs.
kosovo.community: The Kosovar community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated in Dublin and overlapping heavily with the Albanian community. Newcomers usually connect through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, family networks, mosque communities, and football, rather than through any large formal organisation.
kosovo.contrast: Coffee in Pristina is cheap and lasts an afternoon; in Ireland it costs several times more and comes in a paper cup. Rent is the biggest shock, followed by restaurant prices, and nearly everything is paid by card. The climate is mild but wet and dark in winter, and driving is on the left.
kosovo.language: Younger Kosovars often arrive with confident English from school and media, and Irish employers rarely ask for a test certificate. Universities and professional registration bodies do want formal proof, so check early. Irish appears on signs but is not needed in daily life.

moldova.intro: Moldova has a long history of people leaving for work, and Ireland has become a destination for Moldovans in construction, agriculture, hospitality, care and logistics, with a growing number in tech and finance. Many also hold Romanian citizenship, which gives them EU freedom of movement and is part of why the community has grown. Family reunification is common once one person is settled. What surprises many Moldovans is the Irish weather: mild winters with no real snow, cool summers and rain that comes and goes several times a day.
moldova.community: The Moldovan community in Ireland is sizeable and well established, with a strong presence in Dublin and scattered groups in Cork, Limerick and rural towns where agricultural and construction work is. Newcomers tend to find each other through Orthodox church congregations, Romanian-speaking circles, Facebook groups and word of mouth.
moldova.contrast: Fresh produce and markets are a bigger part of life in Moldova than in Ireland, where most shopping is done in supermarkets and costs more. Rent is far higher relative to income, cards are used for almost everything, and evenings happen in the pub. Winters are milder but darker, and you drive on the left.
moldova.language: English ability among Moldovans varies a lot, and many build it on the job alongside Romanian and Russian. Employers rarely ask for a test, though universities and professional registration bodies do. Irish is on signs and paperwork but not needed day to day.

north-macedonia.intro: North Macedonia sends a small but steady number of people to Ireland, mostly for jobs in construction, hospitality and care, along with software developers drawn by the Dublin tech scene and students on English-language and postgraduate courses. Wages, opportunity and family already settled here are the usual reasons, and some come via other EU countries where they first worked. The thing that surprises most Macedonians is how green and wet Ireland is all year round: there are no scorching summers and no real winters, just an endless mild in-between.
north-macedonia.community: The Macedonian community in Ireland is small and recent, centred on Dublin and overlapping with the wider Balkan and ex-Yugoslav circles. Newcomers usually connect through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Orthodox church gatherings, football, and friends of friends rather than through any large formal organisation.
north-macedonia.contrast: Life in Skopje runs late and cheap; in Ireland cafés and shops close early, a meal out costs considerably more, and the evening moves to the pub. Rent takes a much larger share of income, and almost everything is paid by card with tipping kept modest. Driving on the left needs a few weeks of concentration.
north-macedonia.language: Many Macedonians, especially younger ones, arrive with good English from school and subtitled television, and employers usually assess it in interview rather than by certificate. Universities and professional registration bodies do ask for formal scores. Irish is on signs but not needed.

russia.intro: Russia has long supplied Ireland with software engineers, mathematicians, researchers and finance professionals, and the tech multinationals around Dublin remain the main draw, alongside universities, pharma and a smaller number in hospitality and the arts. Many arrive through company transfers or direct hires, others for postgraduate study or to join family, and more recently via a third country where they first relocated. What tends to surprise Russians is how informal and understated Irish life is: small talk everywhere, first names at work, and a strong dislike of anyone appearing too serious.
russia.community: The Russian-speaking community in Ireland is well established and mainly in Dublin, with smaller groups in Cork and Galway, and it spans many nationalities beyond Russia itself. Newcomers usually find each other through Telegram and Facebook groups, Orthodox church parishes, Russian-language weekend schools for children, and cultural events.
russia.contrast: Irish winters are far milder than Moscow but wetter and darker, and you may miss the crisp snowy cold. Rent is expensive and flats are hard to secure, groceries cost more, and you pay by card for almost everything. Shops close early, the pub is the evening's centre, and you drive on the left.
russia.language: Russian professionals in tech and academia usually have strong English, though Irish accents and idioms take a while to decode. Employers judge English at interview; universities and professional registration bodies ask for formal results. Irish is on signs but not needed.

serbia.intro: Serbia has a strong engineering and IT tradition, and Serbians in Ireland cluster in software, data and product roles at the Dublin multinationals, alongside doctors, nurses, tradespeople and hospitality workers. Some arrive through a company transfer, others through healthcare recruitment or a postgraduate course, and family often follows. Wages and opportunity are the honest reasons. What surprises many Serbians most is the Irish evening: the cafés and outdoor terraces of Belgrade have no real equivalent, and social life happens inside the pub, often finishing surprisingly early.
serbia.community: The Serbian community in Ireland is small but active and growing, centred on Dublin with a wider ex-Yugoslav circle that shares events and friendships. Newcomers usually find each other through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Orthodox church gatherings, basketball and football, and colleagues from home.
serbia.contrast: Eating out and coffee cost far more than in Belgrade, and long café afternoons give way to a takeaway cup and a walk in the rain. Rent takes a much larger share of income, cards are used for almost everything, and tipping is light. Winters are mild but dark, and driving is on the left.
serbia.language: Serbians, particularly those in tech and medicine, usually arrive with confident English, helped by years of subtitled television. Employers rarely ask for a formal test, though universities and professional registration bodies do. Irish is on signs but you will not need it.

turkey.intro: Turkey sends a growing number of people to Ireland, drawn by tech and finance jobs in Dublin, postgraduate courses at Irish universities and, most visibly, English-language study, which brings many young Turks to language schools in Dublin, Cork and Galway. Others come as doctors, engineers or academics, or to open or work in restaurants and barbers, and family ties and the wish to live in an English-speaking EU country round out the reasons. What surprises many Turks is the quiet: shops close early, streets empty by evening, and Sunday feels like the whole country has stayed home.
turkey.community: The Turkish community in Ireland is medium-sized and growing, concentrated in Dublin with lively pockets in Cork and Galway around language schools and universities. Newcomers find each other through Turkish student societies, mosque communities, Turkish restaurants and barbers, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, and events organised by the embassy and cultural associations.
turkey.contrast: Tea is still everywhere in Ireland, though it comes with milk rather than in a tulip glass, and the long social evening moves from the çay bahçesi to the pub. Rent is a much heavier burden than in most Turkish cities, groceries and eating out cost more, and payments are almost all by card. Winters are mild but dark and wet, and you drive on the left.
turkey.language: English levels among Turks vary widely, which is why so many come first for language study; those in tech and academia usually arrive fluent. Employers judge English at interview, while universities and professional registration bodies want formal results. Irish is on signs but not needed.

ukraine.intro: Ukraine has a long-standing connection with Ireland through IT outsourcing, agriculture, construction and healthcare, and a steady number of Ukrainian developers, engineers and students were already settling around Dublin before recent events. Since 2022 many more have arrived under temporary protection, spreading across every county rather than only the cities, and finding work in hospitality, care, logistics, tech and education. Family reunion has followed. What surprises many Ukrainians is the Irish winter: almost no snow, mild temperatures, but short grey days and rain that makes it feel colder than it is.
ukraine.community: The Ukrainian community in Ireland is now large and spread across the whole country, from Dublin and Cork to small towns in every county, with a long-established core in Dublin. Newcomers find each other through local Ukrainian support groups, Greek Catholic and Orthodox parishes, Telegram and Facebook groups, and Ukrainian schools and cultural events.
ukraine.contrast: Public transport outside Dublin is thin, and distances that would be a quick marshrutka ride at home may need a car, driven on the left. Rent is high and hard to secure, groceries and eating out cost more, and you pay by card almost everywhere. Shops close early and social life moves indoors to the pub, especially in winter.
ukraine.language: Many Ukrainians, especially in tech, arrive with good English, while others build it through free local classes and work. Employers assess English in conversation, but universities and professional registration bodies require formal test scores. Irish is on signs but not needed.

algeria.intro: Algeria sends a small but growing number of people to Ireland, most often for postgraduate study, research posts and jobs in engineering, IT, pharma and healthcare, with others arriving for English-language courses or to join family. Ireland's appeal is the combination of an English-speaking EU country with a large tech and pharma base, and some come via France, where they first studied or worked. The surprise for most Algerians is the daylight: long, bright summer evenings that last past ten, and winter afternoons that go dark before five.
algeria.community: The Algerian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated in Dublin with a few families in Cork and Galway around the universities and hospitals. Newcomers tend to find each other through mosque communities, the wider Maghrebi and Francophone circles, university societies, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
algeria.contrast: Fresh bread, produce and a hot midday meal are harder to come by; Irish lunches are quick sandwiches and the main meal is in the evening. Rent takes a large share of income, groceries cost more, and everything is paid by card. Winters are mild but grey, halal food needs some seeking out beyond the cities, and driving is on the left.
algeria.language: Algerians usually arrive with French and Arabic and a range of English, from fluent graduates to people still building confidence. Employers judge English in interview, while universities and professional registration bodies want formal results. Irish is on signs but not needed.

bahrain.intro: Bahrain is home to a large expatriate population, so people moving from Bahrain to Ireland are often not Bahraini nationals but Indian, Filipino, British, Pakistani or Arab professionals leaving the Gulf after years there, along with Bahraini students heading to Irish universities, particularly for medicine, which has a long link through the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland's Bahrain campus. Finance, tech, healthcare and hospitality are the usual sectors. The surprise for anyone arriving from Bahrain is not only the cold and the rain but how much of life is lived outdoors regardless of it.
bahrain.community: The Bahraini community in Ireland is very small and mostly made up of medical students and graduates in Dublin, while the wider group of people who have lived in Bahrain is larger and spread across Dublin, Cork and Galway. Newcomers connect through university societies, mosque communities, Gulf alumni networks and WhatsApp groups.
bahrain.contrast: Life in Bahrain runs on cars, air conditioning and late nights; in Ireland you will walk more, dress for rain and find shops closing early. Domestic help and cheap taxis are not part of Irish life, groceries cost more, and payments are by card. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and you drive on the left.
bahrain.language: English is the working language of Bahrain, so most arrivals speak it fluently, though Irish accents and slang take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs but not needed.

egypt.intro: Egypt sends doctors, pharmacists, engineers and software developers to Ireland in steady numbers, with Egyptian doctors in particular a long-established presence in Irish hospitals. Others come for postgraduate study, academic posts, finance jobs or to work in the pharma and medtech plants around Cork and the west, and family often follows once one person is settled. What surprises many Egyptians is the pace of life: everything closes early, the streets are quiet by evening, and the Cairo habit of a late dinner out at midnight simply has no equivalent.
egypt.community: The Egyptian community in Ireland is medium-sized and well established, strongest in Dublin but with a notable presence in Cork, Galway and Limerick because of the hospitals. Newcomers usually connect through mosque communities, Coptic churches, Egyptian doctors' networks, university societies, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
egypt.contrast: Irish daylight is the biggest change: bright summer evenings that stretch past ten and winter darkness by half past four. Rent is expensive and competitive, groceries and eating out cost much more than in Egypt, and almost everything is paid by card. Halal food is easy to find in the cities, less so in small towns, and driving is on the left.
egypt.language: Egyptian professionals in medicine, engineering and tech usually arrive with strong English, though Irish accents take a while. Employers assess English at interview rather than by certificate, while universities and professional registration bodies want formal results. Irish is on signs but not needed.

iran.intro: Iran has a strong academic and engineering culture, and most Iranians in Ireland arrived first as PhD students, postdoctoral researchers or engineers, later moving into tech, pharma, medtech and universities across Dublin, Cork, Galway and Limerick. Others come as doctors or through family, and a calmer life with the chance to build a career in an English-speaking EU country is the usual reason. What surprises many Iranians is how relaxed and unhurried Irish social life is, with plans made loosely, evenings ending early, and small talk about the weather standing in for formality.
iran.community: The Iranian community in Ireland is small but well educated and long-standing, spread across the university cities rather than concentrated in one place. Newcomers tend to find each other through university societies, Nowruz and Yalda gatherings, Persian-language Telegram and WhatsApp groups, and colleagues in tech and research.
iran.contrast: Irish weather is mild all year with none of the hot dry summers of home, and the winter dark comes early. Rent takes a large share of income, groceries and eating out cost more, and cards are used for almost everything. Alcohol is central to pub culture but nobody minds if you drink tea, and driving is on the left.
iran.language: Iranians who come through universities and tech usually have strong English, especially in writing, and employers judge fluency in interview rather than by certificate. Universities and professional registration bodies do ask for formal scores. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

iraq.intro: Iraq sends doctors, dentists, pharmacists, engineers and postgraduate students to Ireland, and Iraqi doctors are a familiar presence in Irish hospitals. Others arrive as academics, in IT or construction, or to join family who settled long ago, and many come via the Gulf, the UK or a scholarship. Stability, career progression and an English-speaking EU country are the usual reasons. What surprises many Iraqis is how quiet and green Ireland is, with small towns, early closing and a pace of life that feels slow after Baghdad or Basra.
iraq.community: The Iraqi community in Ireland is small but established, mostly in Dublin with families in Cork, Galway and Limerick around hospitals and universities. Newcomers usually find each other through mosque communities, Chaldean and other Christian congregations, Iraqi doctors' networks, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
iraq.contrast: Mild, wet weather all year replaces the heat, and winter afternoons go dark early. Rent is high and hard to secure, groceries cost more, and payments are almost all by card. Halal food is straightforward in the cities, the pub is where socialising happens even for those who do not drink, and driving is on the left.
iraq.language: Iraqi professionals in medicine and engineering usually arrive with solid English, though Irish accents and idioms take time. Employers assess English in interview, while universities and professional registration bodies require formal scores. Irish is on signs but is not needed.

israel.intro: Israel sends a small but visible number of people to Ireland, mostly software engineers, product managers and cybersecurity specialists joining the Dublin tech multinationals, along with academics, doctors and a few people opening businesses. Some arrive on company transfers, some through a partner, and many hold a second EU citizenship that makes the move straightforward. What surprises most Israelis is the Irish weather and its effect on life: cool, wet and grey much of the year, with a social scene that moves indoors into pubs rather than onto beaches and terraces.
israel.community: The Israeli community in Ireland is small and largely made up of tech professionals in Dublin, alongside a modest Jewish community with synagogues and a long history in the city. Newcomers usually find each other through work, Hebrew-speaking WhatsApp groups, Jewish community events, and embassy-linked gatherings.
israel.contrast: Sabbath rhythms have no equivalent; the Irish week winds down on Sunday and shops are quieter but open. Rent and eating out are expensive though often no worse than Tel Aviv, groceries cost about as much, and everything is paid by card. Israelis tend to find Irish communication indirect and polite, and driving is on the left.
israel.language: Israelis in tech and academia almost always arrive fluent in English, and employers rarely ask for any certificate, though universities and professional registration bodies do. Irish accents and understated humour take a little decoding. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

jordan.intro: Jordan sends doctors, pharmacists, engineers and students to Ireland, with Jordanian doctors well represented in Irish hospitals and a growing group in tech and finance in Dublin. Postgraduate study at Irish universities is a common route, often followed by a job, and family frequently joins later. Career progression and life in an English-speaking EU country are the usual reasons. What surprises many Jordanians is the daylight: summer evenings bright until ten, winter afternoons dark before five, and the way people plan their year around it.
jordan.community: The Jordanian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, mostly in Dublin with families in Cork, Galway and Limerick around hospitals and universities. Newcomers usually connect through mosque communities, Arab student societies, doctors' networks, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups, alongside the wider Levantine circle.
jordan.contrast: Amman's late dinners and long family evenings give way to early closing and quiet streets. Rent is high and competitive, groceries and eating out cost more, and payments are almost all by card. Halal food is easy to find in the cities, socialising happens in pubs whether or not you drink, and driving is on the left.
jordan.language: Jordanians in medicine, engineering and tech usually arrive with strong English, though Irish accents take time. Employers judge English at interview rather than by certificate, while universities and professional registration bodies require formal results. Irish is on signs but not needed.

kuwait.intro: Kuwait has a large expatriate workforce, so people moving from Kuwait to Ireland are usually Indian, Egyptian, Filipino, Pakistani or Lebanese professionals who have spent years in the Gulf and want a permanent home, along with Kuwaiti students heading to Irish universities, especially for medicine and engineering. Healthcare, tech, finance and construction are the typical sectors. The surprise for anyone arriving from Kuwait is how much of Irish life happens outdoors despite the weather: walking, cycling and standing outside pubs in the rain.
kuwait.community: The Kuwaiti community in Ireland is very small, mostly students and medical graduates in Dublin, while the broader group of people who have lived in Kuwait is larger and spread across the cities.
