Newcomers connect through university societies, mosque communities, Gulf alumni networks and WhatsApp groups of former colleagues.
kuwait.contrast: Life in Kuwait runs on cars, air conditioning and late nights; in Ireland you walk more, dress in layers and find shops closing early. Petrol and domestic help are expensive rather than cheap, groceries cost more, and payments are by card. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and driving is on the left.
kuwait.language: English is the working language in Kuwait, so most arrivals speak it fluently, though Irish accents and slang take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs but not needed.

lebanon.intro: Lebanon has a long tradition of emigration and a strong professional class, and Lebanese in Ireland work in medicine, pharma, finance, tech, engineering and hospitality, with a growing number opening food businesses. Postgraduate study at Irish universities is a common route in, as are company transfers from the Gulf and family already settled. Stability, career progression and an English-speaking EU country are the usual reasons. What surprises many Lebanese is the early evening: restaurants close their kitchens by nine or ten and streets empty long before a Beirut night would even begin.
lebanon.community: The Lebanese community in Ireland is small but established, centred on Dublin with professionals in Cork and Galway around hospitals and pharma. Newcomers usually connect through Maronite and other church communities, mosque communities, university societies, Lebanese restaurants, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
lebanon.contrast: Beirut's café-and-terrace social life has no real match; the Irish equivalent is the pub, with a quieter street outside. Rent is expensive and hard to secure, groceries cost more, and payments are almost all by card. The weather is mild and wet, evenings end early, and you drive on the left.
lebanon.language: Lebanese arrivals usually speak Arabic, French and English, and those in medicine, tech and finance are typically fluent already. Employers judge fluency in interview, while universities and professional registration bodies want formal results. Irish is on signs but you will not need it.

morocco.intro: Morocco sends a small but growing number of people to Ireland, drawn by postgraduate study, research posts, English-language courses and jobs in tech, finance, engineering, hospitality and healthcare, with some arriving via France or Spain where they first studied or worked. Family links and the pull of an English-speaking EU country round out the reasons. What surprises many Moroccans is how quiet and inward Irish evenings are: the medina and café-street bustle has no equivalent, and social life takes place inside pubs, often ending early.
morocco.community: The Moroccan community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, mostly in Dublin with a few families in Cork and Galway around the universities and hospitals. Newcomers usually find each other through mosque communities, the wider Maghrebi and Francophone circles, university societies, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
morocco.contrast: Fresh markets, cheap tagine and long lunches give way to supermarkets, quick sandwiches and an evening main meal that costs more. Rent takes a large share of income, and payments are almost all by card. Halal food is easy in the cities, harder in small towns, the weather is mild but wet, and driving is on the left.
morocco.language: Moroccans usually arrive with Arabic, French and a range of English, from fluent graduates to people still building confidence. Employers judge English at interview, while universities and professional registration bodies require formal results. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

oman.intro: Oman has a large expatriate workforce, so people moving from Oman to Ireland are often Indian, Pakistani, Filipino, British or Arab professionals leaving the Gulf after years there, together with Omani students heading to Irish universities for medicine, engineering and business. Healthcare, tech, finance and hospitality are the usual destinations. The surprise for anyone arriving from Muscat is the weather, of course, but also how small and walkable Irish cities are and how much of life goes on outdoors regardless of the rain.
oman.community: The Omani community in Ireland is very small and mostly made up of students and medical graduates in Dublin, while the broader group of people who have lived in Oman is larger and spread across the cities. Newcomers connect through university societies, mosque communities, Gulf alumni networks and WhatsApp groups.
oman.contrast: Oman's pace is gentler than the rest of the Gulf, so the Irish calm feels less jarring, but the cars, air conditioning and late evenings of Muscat still give way to walking, layers and early-closing shops. Petrol and domestic help are expensive rather than cheap, groceries cost more, payments are by card, weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and driving is on the left.
oman.language: English is widely used in Omani workplaces and universities, so most arrivals speak it well, though Irish accents take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs but not needed.

qatar.intro: Qatar has an expatriate majority, so most people moving from Qatar to Ireland are Indian, Filipino, British, Egyptian or Lebanese professionals who spent years in Doha, plus Qatari students heading to Irish universities, often for medicine or business. Healthcare, tech, finance, construction and aviation are the typical sectors, and many leave the Gulf for a permanent home, better work-life balance and schooling. The surprise for anyone arriving from Doha is how small and informal Ireland feels: no towers, no compounds, and a boss who makes their own tea.
qatar.community: The Qatari community in Ireland is tiny and mostly students in Dublin, while the wider group of people who lived in Qatar is larger and spread across Dublin, Cork and Galway. Newcomers connect through university societies, mosque communities, Gulf alumni networks, and WhatsApp groups of former Doha colleagues.
qatar.contrast: Doha's cars, malls and air conditioning give way to walking, rain jackets and early-closing shops. Petrol and domestic help are expensive rather than cheap, groceries cost more, and payments are by card with light tipping. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and driving is on the left.
qatar.language: English is the working language of Qatar, so most arrivals speak it fluently, though Irish accents and slang take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs but not needed.

saudi-arabia.intro: Saudi Arabia sends students to Ireland in good numbers, particularly for medicine, dentistry, pharmacy, engineering and English-language study, and many Saudi doctors train in Irish hospitals before returning or staying on. Alongside them come expatriate professionals of many nationalities who spent years in the Kingdom and now want a permanent home in an English-speaking EU country, working in healthcare, tech, finance and construction. What surprises most arrivals from Saudi Arabia is the openness of daily life: mixed socialising everywhere, alcohol in pubs, and a relaxed, informal manner in offices and hospitals.
saudi-arabia.community: The Saudi community in Ireland is medium-sized and mostly made up of students and trainee doctors in Dublin, Cork and Galway, with a wider group of former Saudi-based expatriates spread across the country. Newcomers connect through Saudi student clubs, mosque communities, university societies and WhatsApp groups.
saudi-arabia.contrast: Riyadh and Jeddah run on cars, malls and late nights; in Ireland you walk, layer up and find shops shut by evening. Prayer spaces are fewer, halal food takes a little seeking outside the cities, and Friday is an ordinary working day. Groceries cost more, payments are by card, and driving is on the left.
saudi-arabia.language: Saudi students often arrive with intermediate English, which is why so many begin with a language course, while doctors and engineers are usually fluent. Employers judge English at interview, but universities and professional registration bodies require formal scores. Irish is on signs but not needed.

tunisia.intro: Tunisia has a well-educated workforce and sends engineers, software developers, researchers and healthcare workers to Ireland, often via postgraduate study or a first job in France, along with a smaller number in hospitality and finance. English-language study is a growing route for younger Tunisians, and better pay, career prospects and an English-speaking EU country are the usual reasons. What surprises many Tunisians is the Irish summer, which rarely feels like one, and the winter, which is milder than expected but dark and wet in a way that takes real adjusting to.
tunisia.community: The Tunisian community in Ireland is small and recent, mostly in Dublin with a few people in Cork and Galway around tech and universities. Newcomers usually find each other through the wider Maghrebi and Francophone circles, mosque communities, university societies, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
tunisia.contrast: Fresh markets, cheap street food and long lunches give way to supermarkets, quick sandwiches and an evening meal that costs more. Rent is a much bigger share of income, and payments are almost all by card. Halal food is straightforward in the cities, the weather is mild but wet, and driving is on the left.
tunisia.language: Tunisians usually arrive with Arabic, French and a range of English, and those in tech and research are often already fluent. Employers judge English at interview, while universities and professional registration bodies require formal results. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

the-uae.intro: The UAE has an expatriate majority, so most people moving from the UAE to Ireland are Indian, Pakistani, Filipino, British, Egyptian or Lebanese professionals who spent years in Dubai or Abu Dhabi and now want a permanent home, better work-life balance and schooling for children, along with Emirati students heading to Irish universities. Healthcare, tech, finance, aviation and construction are the typical sectors. What surprises most arrivals from the Emirates is how small and informal Ireland feels: no towers, few malls, a boss who makes their own tea, and everyone walking in the rain.
the-uae.community: The Emirati community in Ireland is tiny and mostly students, but the group of people who once lived in the UAE is large and spread across Dublin, Cork and Galway. Newcomers connect through former Dubai colleagues on WhatsApp, university societies, mosque communities, Indian and Filipino associations, and Gulf alumni networks.
the-uae.contrast: Dubai's cars, delivery apps and air conditioning give way to walking, layers and shops that close early. Petrol, taxis and domestic help are expensive rather than cheap, groceries cost more, and everything is paid by card with light tipping. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and driving is on the left.
the-uae.language: English is the working language of the UAE, so most arrivals speak it fluently, though Irish accents and slang take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs, not needed.

angola.intro: Angola sends a small but growing number of people to Ireland, most often via Portugal, where many Angolans first studied or worked before moving on for jobs in construction, healthcare, hospitality, logistics and, increasingly, tech and finance. Postgraduate study and English-language courses bring younger Angolans, and family reunion follows. Better pay and a stable, English-speaking EU country are the usual reasons. What surprises many Angolans is the cold and the dark: not the deep freeze of northern Europe, but a damp mildness and short winter days that make you long for Luanda's light.
angola.community: The Angolan community in Ireland is small and recent, mostly in Dublin and overlapping with the larger Portuguese-speaking and Brazilian communities. Newcomers usually find each other through Portuguese-language churches, Lusophone Facebook and WhatsApp groups, football, and the wider African community networks in the city.
angola.contrast: Luanda is famously expensive for imported goods but cheap for local produce; in Ireland it is closer to the reverse, with supermarket groceries pricey and imported goods ordinary. Rent is hard to secure, payments are almost all by card, and social life lives in the pub. The weather is mild but wet, and driving is on the left.
angola.language: Many Angolans arrive with Portuguese as their first language and English at varying levels, often built up through study or work. Employers judge English at interview, while universities and professional registration bodies require formal scores. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

benin.intro: Benin sends a modest but steady stream of people to Ireland, most often students heading for postgraduate courses, healthcare workers, and IT professionals who have already worked in French-speaking Europe and want an English-speaking base. Some arrive to join a spouse or family member who settled first, and a growing number come through the tech and business services companies in Dublin. What tends to surprise Beninese arrivals most is how early the winter darkness falls and how long the grey, damp days can last before the long, bright summer evenings arrive.
benin.community: The Beninese community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated in Dublin with a few families elsewhere. Newcomers usually find each other through wider francophone West African circles, church congregations, and WhatsApp groups that pass along tips on housing, jobs and where to buy familiar ingredients.
benin.contrast: Compared with Cotonou or Porto-Novo, the biggest daily adjustments are the weather, the cost of renting, and a car-dependent life outside city centres. Cards are accepted almost everywhere and cash is rarely needed. Shops close earlier than you might expect, and much of social life happens in pubs, where a round-buying culture takes a little getting used to.
benin.language: Most Beninese arrive with French as their working language, so building confident professional English matters most for interviews and a clear, concise CV. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but registration bodies and universities often do. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

botswana.intro: Botswana is a small country with a well-educated, English-speaking workforce, and the people who move to Ireland are usually nurses and other healthcare staff, students on postgraduate courses, accountants, and engineers who see Ireland as a friendly first step into Europe. Family ties and a spouse's job bring others. Because Botswana runs on English and a Commonwealth-style institutional culture, the working world feels familiar quickly. The thing that surprises most Batswana is the rain: not its volume so much as its persistence, with a fine drizzle that can last for days and sunlight that feels rationed in winter.
botswana.community: The Botswanan community in Ireland is small and mostly recent, with people spread between Dublin, Cork and hospital towns rather than gathered in one place. Newcomers tend to connect through wider Southern African groups, church congregations, and WhatsApp or Facebook groups, plus occasional events organised with the help of embassy contacts.
botswana.contrast: Driving on the left will feel normal, but the narrow rural roads and constant roundabouts will not. Renting is the biggest shock: viewings are competitive and landlords expect references and a deposit up front. Eating out and takeaways cost more than at home, while groceries in the big supermarket chains are more manageable, and almost everything is paid for by card.
botswana.language: English is an official language of Botswana, so most arrivals are fluent and employers treat you accordingly. Expect a slightly different vocabulary, fast Irish accents that vary by county, and plenty of understatement. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

burkina-faso.intro: Burkina Faso is not a traditional source of migration to Ireland, but a small number of Burkinabè arrive each year, most often as postgraduate students, researchers, healthcare workers, and professionals who have already spent time in France or Belgium and want to work in English. Some come to join family already settled, and a few move within international organisations or tech companies with Dublin offices. The thing that surprises most Burkinabè newcomers is how quiet the streets are in the evening and how much of social life happens indoors, in pubs and homes, rather than outside.
burkina-faso.community: The Burkinabè community in Ireland is very small and largely based in Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through the broader francophone West African network, university international offices, church groups, and WhatsApp groups that circulate advice on rooms to rent and where to find familiar food.
burkina-faso.contrast: After the heat of Ouagadougou, Irish weather is the obvious adjustment, along with short winter days. Renting is expensive and competitive, groceries are dearer than at home, and eating out is a treat rather than a habit. Cards are used for almost everything, shops keep shorter hours, and public transport is thinner outside Dublin, so many people end up driving on the left.
burkina-faso.language: French is the working language for most Burkinabè, so strong professional English is the main preparation for interviews and a clear, concise CV. Irish employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and professional registration bodies usually do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

burundi.intro: Burundi sends only a small number of people to Ireland, and they arrive for varied reasons: postgraduate study, healthcare and care work, family reunification, and in some cases a fresh start after periods of upheaval at home. A few come through international organisations or regional companies with links to Dublin. Many Burundians already speak Kirundi, French and Swahili, so adding English is a familiar kind of challenge. What surprises most is how calm and orderly daily life is, with quiet evenings and a heavy reliance on planning ahead for everything from doctor appointments to buses.
burundi.community: The Burundian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, mostly in Dublin with families in other towns. Newcomers usually find each other through wider East African and Great Lakes networks, church congregations, community centres, and WhatsApp groups, and often mix closely with Rwandan and Congolese neighbours.
burundi.contrast: Coming from Bujumbura's warmth and lakeside light, the grey, wet Irish winter takes real getting used to, and summer evenings stretching late are a pleasant surprise. Renting is costly and paperwork-heavy. Groceries are more expensive, cash is rarely used, and the social centre of many neighbourhoods is the pub rather than the street or the market.
burundi.language: Most Burundians arrive with French and Kirundi rather than English, so confident spoken English is the biggest asset for interviews and everyday admin. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and registration bodies often do. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

cameroon.intro: Cameroon has become one of the more visible African sources of new arrivals in Ireland, with nurses and care workers, engineers, IT professionals and postgraduate students leading the way. Its bilingual system means many Cameroonians already work comfortably in English, which makes Irish hospitals, universities and tech companies a natural fit, and family reunification brings others over time. What tends to surprise new arrivals is how informal Irish workplaces feel, with first names for managers, plenty of humour, and decisions made over tea rather than in formal meetings.
cameroon.community: The Cameroonian community in Ireland is medium-sized and growing, with the largest numbers in Dublin and smaller clusters around Cork, Limerick and hospital towns. People find each other through churches, football matches, cultural associations, and active WhatsApp and Facebook groups, and anglophone and francophone Cameroonians mix freely.
cameroon.contrast: The climate is the first shock, with long, dark winters and a lot of rain, though summers are mild and bright late into the evening. Renting is expensive and competitive, and groceries and eating out cost more than at home. Card payments dominate, tipping is modest, and the pub is where colleagues and neighbours actually get to know you.
cameroon.language: Anglophone Cameroonians usually arrive fluent, while francophone arrivals need confident professional English for interviews and a concise, results-focused CV. Irish employers rarely ask for IELTS, but nursing and other registration bodies and universities often do. Irish is on signs but you will not need it.

the-central-african-republic.intro: The Central African Republic sends only a handful of people to Ireland, and they usually come for study, to join family, or through work with international organisations, healthcare and care roles, or church networks. Some arrive after years in France or Cameroon and want the chance to build an English-speaking career. Because the numbers are so small, newcomers often become the first Central African their Irish neighbours have met. The thing that surprises most is how safe and predictable daily life feels, and how much of it is organised around appointments, timetables and the weather forecast.
the-central-african-republic.community: There is no large Central African community in Ireland, only a small number of families, mostly in Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through wider francophone African networks, churches, community centres and WhatsApp groups, and often find close friends among Cameroonian and Congolese neighbours.
the-central-african-republic.contrast: The cool, wet weather and short winter days are a big change from Bangui, and summer evenings that stay bright late are a welcome surprise. Renting is expensive and requires references. Groceries cost more, eating out is an occasional treat, cards are used for almost everything, and shops close far earlier than you may expect.
the-central-african-republic.language: French and Sango are the everyday languages for most Central Africans, so building confident English is the first priority for interviews and everyday admin. Irish employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and professional bodies often do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

chad.intro: Chad is one of the least common African points of origin for people moving to Ireland, and those who do arrive are usually postgraduate students, staff of international organisations, healthcare and care workers, or people joining family already settled. Some come via France or the Gulf and want an English-speaking country with a growing job market. Given the small numbers, Chadians often find themselves explaining their country to curious colleagues. What surprises most is the sheer greenness of the landscape and how the weather changes several times in a single day.
chad.community: The Chadian community in Ireland is very small, with a few families and students mostly in Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through wider francophone and Muslim African networks, mosques, university international offices and WhatsApp groups rather than through any formal Chadian association.
chad.contrast: After N'Djamena's heat and dust, the damp and the short winter daylight are the biggest adjustments, along with the cost of renting a room or flat. Groceries are dearer than at home, eating out is expensive, and almost everything is paid by card. Working hours are regular and evenings are quiet, with much of social life in pubs and homes.
chad.language: French and Arabic are the main languages for most Chadians, so confident English is the key preparation for interviews and a concise CV. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and professional bodies usually do. Irish is on signs but not needed.

the-republic-of-the-congo.intro: The Republic of the Congo sends a small number of people to Ireland, typically postgraduate students, engineers with oil and gas or construction backgrounds, healthcare workers, and people joining family already in the country. Many have first lived in France or Belgium and see Ireland as a way to build a career in English inside the EU. Newcomers from Brazzaville are often surprised by how informal Irish life is, from first-name terms with senior colleagues to the way strangers strike up conversations at bus stops and in shops.
the-republic-of-the-congo.community: The community from Brazzaville is small and often blends into the larger Congolese community from the DRC, mainly in Dublin. Newcomers find each other through churches, francophone African associations, music and football, and WhatsApp groups that share housing and job tips.
the-republic-of-the-congo.contrast: The weather is the first adjustment: cool, wet winters with short days, then mild summers with long evenings. Renting is expensive and competitive, groceries and eating out cost more than at home, and cards are used almost everywhere. Public transport is limited outside Dublin, so many people end up driving on the left.
the-republic-of-the-congo.language: French and Lingala are the everyday languages for most Congolese arrivals, so strong professional English matters most for interviews and a concise CV. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and registration bodies often do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo.intro: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has one of the older and better-established African communities in Ireland, and people continue to arrive for postgraduate study, healthcare and care work, engineering and IT, family reunification, and in some cases a fresh start after difficult times at home. Many have lived in Belgium or France first and want to build a career in English inside the EU. Congolese newcomers are often surprised by how quiet Irish streets are compared with Kinshasa, and by how much social life happens indoors in pubs, churches and homes.
the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo.community: The Congolese community in Ireland is one of the larger African communities, long-established and centred on Dublin with smaller groups in Cork and other towns. People find each other through lively church congregations, music and dance events, football, cultural associations and busy WhatsApp groups.
the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo.contrast: The cool, damp climate and short winter days are the biggest change from Kinshasa, and the long summer evenings are a real pleasure. Renting is expensive and requires references. Groceries and eating out cost more, cash is rarely used, and the working day is regular and punctual, with the pub as the default place to socialise.
the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo.language: French and Lingala are the everyday languages for most Congolese, so confident English is the main preparation for interviews and a concise CV. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and registration bodies often do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

cote-divoire.intro: Côte d'Ivoire sends a small but growing number of people to Ireland, usually postgraduate students, finance and business graduates, IT professionals, healthcare workers, and people joining family. Abidjan's strong business culture produces plenty of accountants, analysts and engineers who see Dublin's financial services and tech sectors as a natural next step, especially after a stint in France. What surprises Ivorian newcomers most is the pace of the Irish evening: shops and cafés close early, and a night out often ends when the pub does rather than stretching into the small hours.
cote-divoire.community: The Ivorian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, mostly in Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through wider francophone West African networks, church congregations, football matches, university international offices and WhatsApp groups that pass along housing and job tips.
cote-divoire.contrast: The climate is the biggest adjustment, with long, dark winters and frequent rain, though summers are mild and bright late into the evening. Renting is expensive and competitive, groceries and eating out cost more than in Abidjan, cards are accepted everywhere, and public transport is sparse outside Dublin, so driving on the left becomes part of life.
cote-divoire.language: French is the working language for most Ivorians, so building confident professional English is the priority for interviews and a concise, results-focused CV. Irish employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and professional bodies often do. Irish is on signs but not needed.

equatorial-guinea.intro: Equatorial Guinea sends only a very small number of people to Ireland, most often postgraduate students, engineers with oil and gas experience, healthcare workers, and people joining family already in Europe. Many have first lived in Spain and come to Ireland for English-language study or to build a career in an English-speaking EU country. With so few Equatoguineans around, newcomers tend to find their way into wider Spanish-speaking and African networks. What surprises most is the cost and competitiveness of renting and how quickly you need to move when a decent room comes up.
equatorial-guinea.community: There is no established Equatoguinean community in Ireland, just a handful of students and professionals mostly in Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through Spanish-speaking groups, wider African associations, churches, university international offices and WhatsApp groups rather than through a dedicated association.
equatorial-guinea.contrast: The cool, wet weather and short winter days are a marked change from Malabo, though summer evenings stay bright late. Renting is expensive and paperwork-heavy. Groceries cost more than at home, eating out is dearer still, cards are used for almost everything, and much of social life revolves around the pub.
equatorial-guinea.language: Spanish is the everyday language for most Equatoguineans, so confident English is the main preparation for interviews and a concise CV. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and registration bodies often do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

eswatini.intro: Eswatini sends a small number of people to Ireland, most often nurses and other healthcare workers, postgraduate students, teachers and accountants who already work in English and see Ireland as a friendly base for a career in Europe. Family ties and a spouse's job bring others. Because English is an official language at home, the working world here feels familiar quickly, even if the accents do not. What surprises Swazi newcomers most is the winter: not the cold so much as the short, grey days and the way the rain seems to arrive from nowhere.
eswatini.community: The Swazi community in Ireland is small and recent, spread between Dublin, Cork and hospital towns rather than gathered in one area. Newcomers usually find each other through wider Southern African groups, church congregations, and WhatsApp or Facebook groups, and often mix with South African neighbours.
eswatini.contrast: Driving on the left is the same as at home, but Irish roads are narrower and roundabouts are everywhere. Renting is the big adjustment: viewings are competitive and landlords expect references. Groceries are manageable in the big chains, eating out costs more than in Mbabane, and card payments are the norm almost everywhere.

lesotho.intro: Lesotho sends a small number of people to Ireland, most often nurses and other healthcare workers, postgraduate students, teachers and accountants who already work in English and see Ireland as a welcoming base for a career in Europe. Scholarship students in public health, agriculture and development are common, as are nurses and doctors who train or gain experience here. Dar es Salaam's professional class also sees Ireland as an English-speaking route to EU careers. What surprises most Tanzanians first is how quiet and empty streets are in the evening and how early everything closes compared with Dar.
tanzania.community: The Tanzanian community in Ireland is small but friendly and slowly growing, based mainly in Dublin with students and health workers in Galway, Cork and Limerick. Newcomers usually connect through East African and Swahili-speaking groups, church congregations, mosques, university societies, embassy cultural events and WhatsApp groups shared by fellow students.
tanzania.contrast: Ireland's cool, wet, windy weather and short winter days are the biggest daily shift from Tanzania's heat and steady year-round daylight. Renting is formal and competitive, groceries and eating out cost more, and bargaining does not exist. Card payments dominate where mobile money would at home, and driving is on the left, which will feel familiar.
tanzania.language: English is widely used in Tanzanian secondary and higher education, so most arrivals manage interviews well, though everyday Irish accents and slang take time. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and professional registration bodies may. Irish is on signs but not needed.

togo.intro: Togo is a small and recent source of arrivals to Ireland, mostly students, healthcare and care workers, hospitality staff and young professionals in tech and finance, many of whom lived in France or Germany first. Lomé's francophone graduates often choose Ireland precisely to work in English inside the EU, and some come through family or church connections. Others arrive after study in Ghana or Nigeria with English already in hand. What surprises most Togolese first is the cost of a simple meal out and how much cooking at home becomes part of life.
togo.community: The Togolese community in Ireland is very small and recent, almost entirely in Dublin with a few families and students in Cork and Galway. Newcomers usually connect through wider West African and francophone associations, Catholic and evangelical congregations, football, and WhatsApp groups rather than a dedicated Togolese organisation.
togo.contrast: Lomé's heat and sea air are replaced by cool drizzle, wind and winter days that end mid-afternoon, while summer evenings stay light until late. Renting is formal and competitive, groceries and eating out cost noticeably more, and street food barely exists. Cards are used for almost everything, and driving is on the left.
togo.language: Most Togolese arrive with French and Ewe or Kabiyè as their main languages, so English is usually the main adjustment; employers judge it in interviews rather than through IELTS, while universities and registration bodies may want one. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

uganda.intro: Uganda has deep links with Ireland through long-standing Irish aid programmes, missionaries and university partnerships, and Ugandans come for postgraduate study, nursing and care work, medicine, tech and NGO roles, and to join family already here. Kampala's large English-speaking graduate population makes Ireland a natural next step, especially for health professionals and public-health researchers. Some arrive via the UK, where Ugandan communities are larger. What surprises most Ugandans first is the silence: how quiet neighbourhoods are at night and how few people are out on the street after dark.
uganda.community: The Ugandan community in Ireland is modest but well organised and growing, with most people in Dublin and clusters around hospitals and universities in Cork, Galway and Limerick. Newcomers find each other through church congregations, Ugandan community and student associations, independence celebrations, football and netball, and WhatsApp groups.
uganda.contrast: Kampala's warm, evenly split days give way to cold rain, wind and dark winter afternoons, with summer evenings that stay bright until late. Renting is formal and competitive, groceries and eating out cost much more, and boda-bodas are replaced by buses, bikes and long walks. Cards dominate over cash and mobile money, and driving is on the left as at home.
uganda.language: English is Uganda's official language and most arrivals speak it fluently, so interviews are rarely a problem beyond adjusting to Irish accents and understatement. Employers do not usually ask for IELTS, though registration bodies and universities may. Irish is on signs but not needed.

zambia.intro: Zambia has friendly, long-standing links with Ireland through Irish missionaries, teachers and aid workers, and Zambians now move here for nursing and care work, medicine, engineering, postgraduate study and family. English-medium education makes Irish hospitals, universities and offices accessible, and a growing number of Zambian graduates also arrive via the UK or South Africa. Scholarships in public health, agriculture and development remain a common first step. What surprises most Zambians first is how formal and slow renting is compared with simply finding a place through a friend in Lusaka.
zambia.community: The Zambian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated in Dublin with health workers and students in Cork, Limerick and Galway. Newcomers connect through church congregations, wider Southern African groups, university societies, football and braai gatherings, and WhatsApp and Facebook groups where housing and job tips circulate.
zambia.contrast: Lusaka's sunny, dry-season winters and reliable warmth are replaced by cool rain and short dark winter days, though summer evenings run late. Groceries, rent and eating out cost considerably more, and load-shedding is not something you will plan around. Cards are used for nearly everything, distances are short, and driving on the left will feel familiar.
zambia.language: English is Zambia's official language and most arrivals speak it fluently, so interviews are rarely a problem beyond adjusting to Irish accents and slang. Employers seldom ask for IELTS, though nursing and other registration bodies and universities may. Irish is on signs but not needed.

zimbabwe.intro: Zimbabwe has become one of the more visible African sources of arrivals in Ireland, driven above all by nursing, care work, medicine and allied health, alongside accountancy, engineering, IT, postgraduate study and family reunification. Many Zimbabweans come directly from Harare or Bulawayo, while others move on from the UK or South Africa where communities are larger. English-medium schooling and a strong professional culture make the transition into Irish workplaces relatively smooth. What surprises most Zimbabweans first is how relaxed and first-name Irish offices and hospitals are, even between junior staff and senior managers.
zimbabwe.community: The Zimbabwean community in Ireland is well established and still growing, spread beyond Dublin into Cork, Limerick, Galway and many regional towns thanks to healthcare jobs. Newcomers find each other through Pentecostal and Catholic congregations, Zimbabwean community groups, braais, cricket and football, and active Facebook and WhatsApp groups.
zimbabwe.contrast: Harare's dry sunshine and long bright days become cool rain and winter afternoons that end early, with summer evenings stretching late. Groceries, eating out and rent cost more, and renting is formal and competitive. Cards and contactless dominate, there are no power cuts to plan around, and driving on the left will feel like home.
zimbabwe.language: English is the language of education and work in Zimbabwe, and most arrivals speak it fluently, so interviews are rarely an issue beyond Irish accents. Employers do not usually ask for IELTS, though registration bodies and universities may. Irish is on signs but not needed.

bangladesh.intro: Bangladesh sends growing numbers to Ireland for postgraduate study in computing, engineering, data science and business, followed by jobs in tech, hospitality, retail, healthcare and accountancy. Dhaka's large graduate population sees Ireland as an English-speaking, EU-based route to an international career, and many arrive on university courses in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway before moving into work. What surprises most Bangladeshis first is the quiet: how empty streets, buses and shops feel next to Dhaka's constant motion.
bangladesh.community: The Bangladeshi community in Ireland is modest but well established and growing, with most people in Dublin and student clusters in Cork, Limerick and Galway. Renting is formal, competitive and expensive, and eating out costs far more than at home. Cards dominate, bargaining does not happen, pubs are the centre of social life even for non-drinkers, and driving is on the left as at home.

Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and professional registration bodies usually do. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

cambodia.intro: Cambodia is a small and recent source of arrivals in Ireland, mostly students on scholarships or self-funded master's courses, hospitality and restaurant workers, and a few professionals in tech and development organisations. Irish NGO and church links with Cambodia go back a long way, and some people come through those networks or through family already in Europe. Phnom Penh's young, internationally minded graduates increasingly look beyond Australia to English-speaking EU options. What surprises most Cambodians first is the cold and the wind, and the way Irish people cheerfully carry on outdoors regardless of the rain.
cambodia.community: The Cambodian community in Ireland is very small and recent, concentrated in Dublin with a scattering of students in Cork and Galway. Newcomers usually connect through wider Southeast Asian groups, Buddhist gatherings, university international societies and WhatsApp groups, and often rely on Thai, Vietnamese and Filipino networks for food and friendship.
cambodia.contrast: Phnom Penh's heat and short, sharp downpours give way to cool damp weather in every season and dark winter afternoons. Renting is formal and competitive, food and eating out cost far more, and street food and late-night markets barely exist. Cards are used for nearly everything, and driving is on the left rather than the right.
cambodia.language: English proficiency varies: many young Cambodian graduates and hospitality workers speak it well, while others need time to build confidence. Employers judge English in interviews rather than through IELTS, but universities and registration bodies usually want a certificate. Irish is on signs but not needed.

china.intro: China is one of the largest sources of students and skilled workers in Ireland, with people arriving for undergraduate and postgraduate study, then for tech, finance, pharma, engineering, accountancy and research roles across Dublin, Cork, Galway and Limerick. Ireland's English-speaking universities, its concentration of global tech and pharma employers and its EU access make it a popular choice for graduates from Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou and beyond. china.community: The Chinese community in Ireland is large and long-established, centred on Dublin with substantial student and professional groups in Cork, Galway, Limerick and Maynooth. Newcomers find each other through university Chinese student and scholar associations, WeChat groups for every city and topic, Chinese-language churches, Spring Festival events and Irish-Chinese cultural and business organisations.

Renting is competitive and formal, groceries and eating out cost more, and mobile payment apps give way to cards. Delivery is slower and pricier, pubs anchor social life, and driving is on the left.
china.language: Most Chinese arrivals have strong written English from school and university, and spoken confidence grows quickly in daily use; Irish accents and slang take time. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and registration bodies usually do. Irish is on signs but not needed.

hong-kong.intro: Hong Kong has a close and growing link with Ireland, with people moving for tech, finance, accountancy, law, healthcare and university study, and a noticeable wave of families arriving in search of an English-speaking, EU-based life. Long-standing ties through Irish schools and religious orders in Hong Kong mean many arrivals already know Irish names and institutions. Dublin's financial services and tech sectors are the main draws, with Cork and Galway attracting pharma and medtech professionals. What surprises Hong Kongers most is the pace: shorter working hours, relaxed deadlines and shops that close before dinner.
hong-kong.community: The Hong Kong community in Ireland is growing quickly and increasingly visible, mainly in Dublin with families in Cork, Galway and commuter towns. Newcomers connect through Hong Konger community groups, Cantonese-speaking churches, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for housing and schools, and the older Chinese restaurant and business networks.
hong-kong.contrast: Hong Kong's humidity, dense high-rises and round-the-clock convenience give way to cool wet weather, low-rise suburbs and early closing hours. Renting feels chaotic and competitive but flats are bigger, groceries and eating out cost more, and public transport is thinner. Cards replace Octopus, driving is on the left as at home, and pubs replace cha chaan tengs as the default meeting place.
hong-kong.language: Most Hong Kongers arrive with fluent English from school and work, so interviews are straightforward; employers will not ask for IELTS, though universities and professional registration bodies may. Irish accents and slang take a few weeks, and Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Cards are used for almost everything, driving is on the left as at home, and pubs are where socialising happens, even over soft drinks.

Employers judge English in interviews rather than through IELTS, but universities and professional registration bodies usually require a certificate. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Irish accents take time, and Irish is on signs but not needed.

Cards dominate over cash, marshrutkas are replaced by buses, and driving is on the left.
